newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude ends sharply lower on expiry.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude ends sharply lower on expiry.

text.p: NYMEX crude tumbled Tuesday as traders scrambled to liquidate positions in the expiring May crude contract, erasing healthy gains of the past several sessions and ignoring a workers strike that threatened crude supply in Nigeria.

"My feeling is we went up on some position strategies ahead of the expiry, and now it has dropped back to the $19.00 to $20.00 range which I think better matches the (crude) supply situation," said Pat Hughes, market analyst with Chevron Corp in California.
May crude ended 78 cents a barrel lower at $19.60.
Caught in crude's downdraft, May gasoline settled 1.03 cents a gallon lower at 61.77 cents while May heating oil settled down 0.65 cent a gallon at 54.83 cents.

Hughes said refiners have been able to absorb some of the crude surplus in the U.S. Gulf that occurred earlier this month due to an influx of imports, but he said there is still a comfortable amount of crude available.

In fact, dealers expected that weekly oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) to be released Tuesday evening would show a build in crude stocks of about one million barrels, mainly due to imports.

But, imports could be curtailed from West Africa soon due to a strike by contractors that handle the berthing and loading of tankers in Nigeria. The strike has caused a delay but no cancellations of Royal Dutch Shell's Bonny light exports, said Royal Dutch Shell Tuesday. Shell's bonny output is about half of the roughly 950,000 barrels per day it produces in Nigeria.
Several brokers were said to have liquidated significant long positions in the May/June spread after an expected widening of the spread's backwardation never materialized.

May/June had moved from contango April 14 to a 31 cent backwardation on Monday primarily on short covering ahead of the May contract expiry. Since last Wednesday, prompt crude had gained more than a dollar a barrel.

Contango means the nearer contract is cheaper than the later one and backwardation means the nearer contract is more expensive. June crude, the new spot month, opens Wednesday only two cents over July.
Some chartists expect June crude will be able to hold a shelf of support set by eight-month lows made early to mid-April that stood at $19.08, $19.10, and $19.13.
"We are at a time of year when prices usually bottom, and there is a good deal of support in the $19.10 area which should hold," said Jake Bernstein, president of MBH Commodity Advisors in Illinois.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
